channel.name: Hear His Voice
channel.description: A reverent short-form channel that lets Scripture speak for itself. Each episode is one passage of the World English Bible Catholic, read verbatim by a calm, warm narrator over cinematic stock footage, with the exact words captioned on screen. The viewer should feel as though they are hearing a living word rather than watching a video. NEVER sensational, NEVER clickbait, NEVER used out of context to manipulate. The Scripture is the star; the visuals only serve it.

scripture.scope: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John only. This limit is enforced in code, not by any list. The channel reads these four Gospels SEQUENTIALLY, rotating Matthew -> Mark -> Luke -> John, and each book continues from the next unread verse - so nothing decides what comes next except the reading position itself.

source.attribution: The World English Bible is in the Public Domain. Copyright status: public domain. 'World English Bible' is a trademark of eBible.org. The text may be copied, published, broadcast, monetized, and redistributed; it must not be altered and still be called the World English Bible.
notes: Midvash (https://api.midvash.com) was evaluated first and does NOT serve WEBC. GET /v1/versions?language=en returns 11 English translations and WEBC is not among them; GET /v1/versions/webc returns VERSION_NOT_FOUND. Midvash only serves the Protestant 'web' translation, which is a different translation set. The official WEBC USFM release from eBible.org is therefore used instead of silently substituting another translation.
The archive is downloaded once and cached under media/cache/scripture. It is the source of truth for every word spoken or captioned.

content_generation.scripture_scope_note: Episodes come only from Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. That limit is enforced in code, not by the shape of any list. The scripture block below holds the WEBC source and the guidance examples; the passages themselves are drawn from the entire Gospel text at runtime.
visual_rules: Generate one practical Pexels stock-footage search query per spoken segment. The viewer will hear the Scripture while seeing this footage, so the query must support the meaning of that specific segment without pretending to be the event itself.
Keep every query short, generally 2-5 words, using concrete nouns a human editor would actually type into Pexels.

Prefer scenes that exist as real stock footage: landscapes, light and weather, hands and craft, roads and journeys, water, fire, bread, hands raised in prayer, people listening, a lamp burning, an open book, fields at harvest.

Do NOT search for the literal miracle or person. There is no stock footage of Jesus, and queries like 'Jesus healing' or 'biblical drama' return unusable results. Search for the FEELING or SYMBOL the passage carries: 'light breaking through clouds', 'still water at dawn', 'a single candle in darkness', 'hands opening a letter'.
Do not invent specific named people, faces of actors playing biblical figures, or shots that could only exist as CGI. The footage must look like beautiful, reverent real-world cinematography.
Test each query mentally: if I typed this into Pexels, would several genuinely usable vertical clips come back? If not, choose a more practical phrase.
Avoid graphic, violent, frightening, or distressing imagery. Nothing should be horror, gore, wreckage, or disaster. The register is calm, dignified, and hopeful.

Avoid anything that would look wrong next to the Word of God: neon club lighting, arcade machines, fast cars, smartphones, modern corporate offices, meme-style reactions, text overlays, or watermarks.
Vary the queries across the episode so no two consecutive segments look alike. Avoid repeating the same noun more than twice.
When in doubt, choose the quieter, more timeless image. Light, sky, water, stone, wood, linen, bread, and hands are always safe.
creative_directions: You are directing the visuals for Scripture that is being read word for word. Your job is to make the viewer feel the passage, not to explain it.
Each segment's visual_direction is a single sentence describing the shot the viewer should see, in a reverent, cinematic, contemplative register.
Let the direction follow the passage's emotional movement: begin in stillness or question, build toward light and warmth, and settle into quiet resolve.
Favour natural light, shallow depth of field, slow camera movement, and calm negative space. Think of reverent documentary photography rather than dramatic action.
Do not use religious iconography that would be cheap or kitsch: no glowing halos, no beams of light from heaven, no cartoon angels, no stained-glass clichés, no crosses as decoration.
Honour the text's setting where it is filmable: hillsides, olive groves, the shore of a lake, stone streets, a lamplit room, a field, a road, a table set with bread.

The direction must never contradict or trivialize what is being said. If a verse is about comfort, the frame should feel like comfort; if it is about warning or urgency, the frame should feel sober and clear rather than frightening.
